name: Tyrosine supplements for tanning

card.summary: Amino-acid pills or lotion sold on the idea that more raw material means more melanin, with no human tanning trials behind it.
card.note: Tyrosine does not replace UV exposure for tanning; UV exposure carries skin cancer risk.

quick.overview:
L-tyrosine is a common amino acid and a building block of melanin. Some tanning products and supplement sellers suggest taking it orally or applying it topically to boost tanning.

No published human studies have tested whether it changes tanning or skin colour.
quick.mechanism: Melanocytes convert tyrosine into melanin after UV exposure. Proponents reason that extra tyrosine supplies more raw material; research has not tested whether this changes pigment in people.
quick.risks: Tyrosine is sold as a dietary supplement. Tanning itself involves UV exposure, which is classified as a carcinogen and causes sunburn and skin ageing.

lead: Tyrosine supplements for tanning is the practice of taking L-tyrosine, a standard amino acid, as pills or applying it in lotions to help the skin darken or tan faster. The appeal is cosmetic: a deeper, more even tan from less sun, or a tan for people who say they tan slowly.[3][4] The idea rests on tyrosine's role as the starting material for melanin, the pigment made by melanocytes.[1][2]

Tyrosine is a conditionally essential amino acid that the body makes from phenylalanine and obtains from protein-rich foods; it is also sold as a dietary supplement and is a precursor of neurotransmitters such as dopamine.[1] Tanning involves increased melanin production after UV exposure.[2] Bodybuilding forums have long carried the suggestion: a 2008 T Nation thread advised a few grams of L-tyrosine for people who have trouble tanning, and a poster in a 2009 thread described adding it to a sun routine alongside melanotan.[4][5]

The idea resurfaced on social media, where dermatologists quoted by New Beauty described it as a TikTok claim without supporting evidence, noting that tanning depends on more than the amount of melanin precursor available.[3] Published research on supplemental tyrosine has concentrated on cognition and stress rather than pigmentation.[1]

chain: Tyrosine is the raw material for melanin
Supplement is taken before or around sun exposure
angle.text: Users take or apply tyrosine hoping to supply extra melanin precursor so that sun or tanning-bed exposure produces a darker tan.[4][5] Any tan still requires UV exposure, which is the trigger for melanin production.[2]

infobox: Faster or deeper tanning via melanin production[3][4]
Meat, fish, dairy, eggs, some nuts and seeds[1]
Acetyl tyrosine in some topical tanning products[3]
Not approved by the FDA for tanning, per New Beauty[3]

paras: Tyrosine is one of the 20 standard amino acids and a precursor of melanin as well as of dopamine and norepinephrine.[1] Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation, and tanning is increased melanin production after UV exposure.[2] Dermatologist Stacy Chimento, quoted in New Beauty, explained that the body converts L-tyrosine to melanin via the enzyme tyrosinase.[3]

sections.h: Use in tanning and bodybuilding communities
paras: Supplement marketing points to the melanin pathway as a reason extra substrate could support more pigment.[3] In forum posts from 2008 and 2009, T Nation users recommended taking L-tyrosine before sun exposure, noting it was already an ingredient in some pre-workout products, and another poster listed it as a first step before getting sun alongside melanotan II and vitamin D.[4][5]

New Beauty reports that a study in Comprehensive Series in Photosciences found oral L-tyrosine did not induce tanning or enhance UVB-induced tanning, and that a Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology paper reported tyrosine pills had not been shown to work.[3] Dermatologists quoted there Jacquiline Habashy and Deborah Longwill said the claim lacks support and that tanning depends on several factors besides melanin production.[3]

No studies found of tyrosine as a tanning aid that this wiki could cite directly. The New Beauty article cites a study in which oral L-tyrosine did not induce tanning or enhance UVB-induced tanning.[3] Research on supplemental tyrosine in healthy people has otherwise examined cognition and mood under demanding conditions, with a 2015 systematic review concluding it may benefit working memory under stress.[1]

Supplemental tyrosine is widely sold as a dietary supplement.[1] New Beauty notes the FDA has not approved L-tyrosine for tanning, and Chimento notes that L-tyrosine can also be converted to compounds that may affect mood and stress responses.[3] Tanning itself requires UV exposure, whose health risks, including skin cancer, are documented separately.[2]

lore.intro: The tyrosine-for-tanning idea appears in bodybuilding forum threads as a tip for people who tan poorly.[4][5]

claims.claim: A few grams of L-tyrosine before sun exposure helps you tan.
claims.believers: A 2008 T Nation poster recommended taking a large dose of L-tyrosine for tanning trouble, describing it as a melanin precursor and noting that it also lets users still get vitamin D from the sun.[4] Another poster listed it as an extra step in a sun routine.[5]
claims.experts: A study reported by New Beauty found oral L-tyrosine did not induce tanning or enhance UVB-induced tanning, and dermatologists quoted there said the claim lacks evidence.[3]
